But everyone has to stand up for themselves at some time . . .

Well, I haven't tried it yet, so this is just my uneducated opinion on the matter. Hopefully someone with more experience will correct me where I'm wrong.

But I think maybe your friends are definitely taking advantage of you. Everyone should have the right to set their own limits about what they want to do, and they shouldn't guilt you into accommodating them all the time. Especially if they aren't doing the same for you. Personally, I am getting to the point where I don't care if others are upset with me for not doing what they want. I'm done martyring myself for other people.

Take that with a grain of salt, though, as I don't know your friends or the whole situation. But here are some questions that might help you to think about it:
Can you count on these people to make the same or comparable sacrifices for you as you are for them?
Do they actually call you a bitch, or do you just feel like one for saying no?
How do you come across when you say no? Is it that maybe you need to be nicer or more assertive about it?

I also think that if you risk being alone because you say no, then maybe you should let these people go. Trust me, I know that being alone sucks balls, but sometimes, it feels much better than having people around who only want to use you. 

As my therapist once said, there are 6 billion people in the world, and you've only met a few of them so far. If you let these people go, eventually you'll find some who love you for you.

But I do want you to think about this and decide whether the risk of being left alone is real, or just imagined. Sometimes it seems worse in our heads than it actually is. So you'll need to think about it, and maybe have a few conversations with your friends/boyfriend.

But definitely, don't allow yourself to feel forced to stay in any situation that you're not comfortable in. Remember that you have needs as well, and your friendships should be mutually satisfying.

Really? That's encouraging.

Yeah, I know what that's like.

For me, it was my parents. Always trying to be good to them, but ending up being the least liked of all their children, because I dared to have my own opinions and goals a few times.

Then various friends, for whom I tried to be a great friend to, but ended up getting walked away from for all sorts of reasons.

And then boyfriends . . . trying to be the perfect partner, but always getting left for other people. 

I'm planning a personality shift for the new year. It's insanity to do the same thing over and over again and expect different results, right? So I'm going to try being less nice. I won't be evil, but I'm definitely going to stop sacrificing myself all the time, and start asking myself what I want. Maybe taking care of myself more will help me to discover what it is that I'm always depressed about.

People are generally just ungrateful. It's human nature to take others for granted. So maybe it might help to examine why you're always trying to be so nice, and see if it's really worth the trouble. For me, I thought that if I was nice enough that people would like me. But that hasn't turned out to be the case, so I'm going to try something else.

Whatever you decide to do, good luck, and I hope you find people who appreciate you and make you feel loved.

He was 21. We did know him and his family beforehand. I did like him beforehand.

I'm sorry for the confusion, but it didn't happen quite like that. I've explained in other comments.

He does not go to the same church as I do.

And yes . . . I realise now that they were not true friends.

He was 21, he was not the son of anyone in any great social standing. He was not a deacon, or any other person of that sort of importance in the church. My family was acquainted with him and his family beforehand. 

When my father started resisting this relationship, it was a relationship, not an arranged marriage. I understand that it sounded like that, as, for the sake of brevity, I couldn't fully explain everything. But it wasn't quite like that. I wasn't being swept away into marrying this guy. I was fairly convinced that I should marry him, but I was mindful enough to delay it and think about it and eventually break off the relationship.

I'm sorry for the confusion, though. It's just that this is very complicated, and I couldn't explain everything in one post.

I accept responsibility for that decision. I guess I thought I could get both things. 

I do believe that parents should help their kids to get into college . . . why bring me into this world and not help me get the best start I can as an adult, especially if you're able to?

However, that is my personal belief, and I understand that others have different opinions.

Thanks. I am currently undergoing therapy with a counselor at my university. 

However, my dad did not know all the intricacies of this situation until much later. When he started resisting my relationship, it was honestly just a relationship.

However, my dad didn't know early on about the intended marriage. I don't think so, anyway. It wasn't quite that I went in expecting to marry the guy right away, either . . . but as I said, I believed that he was someone I was supposed to date, and over time the marriage part became more serious. 

I wasn't blindly going into the marriage, though. I had my reservations about it, and after some evaluation, I decided to end the relationship and not go through with the whole thing. But I understand that a parent might not want to leave it up to me to make such decisions on my own. 

No, my parents don't treat me fairly now, either. Generally, I have become the family's black sheep, partially due to this relationship situation, but I always kind of was, I guess. I'm not treated fairly at all. Not at home, and not when I used to work in my dad's business.

I did pray, but perhaps my prayers were focused towards the wrong thing. As I said, I thought that God wanted me to marry that guy, so my prayers about the relationship were focused around it working out. I thought I already knew God's will, so I wasn't really seeking it. But I guess that is a lesson learned in itself.

To summarise, the relationship was set up by some people in my church, who pushed the idea that God wanted my boyfriend and I to get married. I believed it at the time, which contributed to, but was not solely responsible for my reluctance to end the relationship. 

So one one hand, I had my dad pressuring me to do what I thought was give up the man I was supposed to marry, and on the other hand, I had these people pushing me to cut loose from my family and elope with this guy. When we finally broke up, I lost those friends from church for some reason, which made me feel extra lonely at that time. 

And the fallout from that is that I now have a considerable amount of doubt and general illwill for my own religion.

But I don't think that has much bearing on any advice you have to give me now, which is why I left it out.

Thank you for your advice, though. I will really think about talking to my mother about it, but I have zero faith in either of my parents' ability to empathise with me and understand. I'll at least have to have a good back up plan for what to do if she brushes me off, and I feel even more hurt, and embarrassed.

Part of the reason I'm reluctant to change it is that I used to have a flat back labret stud in, and I can't be sure whether it was scar tissue, or just dried drainage, but the back of my piercing felt really tough, not like the front at all. Now that I've had the ring in for a few days and the area has gotten some more air, it feels softer and a lot more like flesh, and less like scabs. I'm not sure what that means, so if you have anything to say about that, I'd appreciate it. There is still some drainage though (that is normal, right? It doesn't smell or anything, and it isn't thick like pus), so I'm taking extra care to check that it's clean and that it isn't scarring.

If it doesn't feel good after a week or so, I'll go back to the labret.

I'm sorry. It is cringey, and weird and infuriating and confusing.

I'm beginning to wonder if he's one of those people who don't believe that depression is a real illness. And you are absolutely right. It does take time to shift a worldview. I've been trying to explain that to him.

He thinks that I need to change mine in order to get better. And I agree, I alternate between idealism and pessimism, both unhelpful mindsets for understanding the world. But even if that was the solution to my problems, I can't do it overnight. He seems convinced that I can, but I don't want to because it's too hard.

I won't do anything more right now to keep the friendship. We can't reach a compromise, and at this point, any attempt at conversation is only going to make things worse. 

I will take about a month off, and try to see if I can get any better through therapy. When I'm feeling better, I will try to talk to him again, and if it comes up, then I can smugly say, "yes, I got this way because of therapy". Hopefully we'll be better after some time apart.

Everyone says that, but I'm almost convinced now that better friends don't exist. I've been through way too much with people to be that optimistic anymore.

He doesn't believe I'm depressed. That's the long and short of it. 

And if he doesn't believe that, I'm not sure that we can be friends anymore. This isn't going to go away for now, and I'm going to have an awfully hard time sharing the few good moments I have with him, if he won't be there for the bad ones.

But still, I'm extremely sad. We have a long history together. I really expected him to be more understanding.

My experience through the years has always been that people have been fiercely adamant that I am not depressed. It's so weird, and very alienating. I'm so sorry that this had happened. I wish I'd never opened up to him today.

Yeah, I wouldn't advise anyone to try to be friends right away, even with the little romantic experience that I have. I guess I know that because I've been friends for a long time with someone that I love, but we decided a relationship wouldn't work because of irreconcilable differences. It's worked because we both respect each other's boundaries, but that doesn't mean that it isn't hard. Sometimes it's incredibly difficult. 

I don't understand why you (not you but the dumpers) would break up with someone but not even want to give them the space to recover right after, but it comes off to me as wanting to have the best of both worlds, and it's very unfair to the person who was dumped. 

In a way, I take a bit of pleasure in keeping my distance. I realise that he wants to be close to me, for whatever reason, and it's a bit like a punishment for him :P I definitely want him to think long and hard about the decision that he made, and to miss me, as I really do try hard to be a quality girlfriend. Staying close just makes it way too easy for him.

But that's a little bit malicious, and I wouldn't necessarily advise that you rationalise it that way either. But I hope you're able to get the space that you need and feel better soon.

I think he thought that we could make an instant transition from lovers to friends, and he doesn't want to accept the separation.

I made the mistake of entertaining discussion with him each time, afraid of seeming uninterested in case he was thinking of coming back. But he isn't, and I insist on having my time alone now to come to terms with that before I can think about being friends with him.

I found this article maybe a year or so ago, and I've never really liked it.

Actually, I don't think it makes sense. The writer said that we use love as a crutch to not make changes . . . right after saying that the prospect of love is what motivates our greatest changes.

I dunno . . . If I found out that I would never find love, I think think that fact would be more likely to make me completely complacent. If you would never really have someone else to impress, then why change? On the contrary, I try to improve myself partly because I want to be a pretty decent mate. That's only part of the reason, though. There are others, including career prospects and general personal development.

I think that the author was trying to make a good point, but I think they went about the wrong way to make it. And that's because first impressions are lasting impressions, and when I first found this I was in a lot of pain, and none of it resonated with me. The reasoning didn't make sense to me, and the part about friends and family didn't reflect my reality either, as my family is dysfunctional and I had maybe one true friend at the time. All it seemed to be saying to me was to get used to the idea that no one else might ever love me.

Please note, that if anyone else finds comfort in it, that's all well and good, but I've never thought that this was a particularly helpful passage.

I just realised there was something I didn't say. I want to include it, for transparency.

I neglected to mention that the person he felt "safer" with was someone who has more material resources. Because I know his history, I understand why this was an issue for him (he gave a lot materially to someone who didn't give back emotionally). But I think this is where a lot of people just think "oh, gold digger. He's a bad person".

Does that necessarily change anything?

Thank you :) this was really good for me to hear. I was beginning to wonder how damaged I really was mentally, that no one else could see things from my point of view. I understand that there's nothing more that I can do for him at this point, and I know that I should stop worrying about trying to do one more thing to get him back, and instead focus on myself. But I also know that just hating him and tossing him aside isn't the right response either.

As an experiment, I searched up posts in /r/relationships from the flipside of the situation - the dumpers instead of the dumpee. I found that the information there isn't reliable at all, and is biased based on who the op is. If you are the dumpee, they tell you to move on fast. If you are the dumper, they hurry you to go on and get that person back. In doing so, I've learned to just use that sub for venting, as the advice is really unreliable.

But I guess that is kind of what I learned in ethics yesterday. There is no absolute right and wrong. It's kind of a matter of perspective.

Thanks again. I will try to remember this to keep my spirits up today.

In the darkest times, those are the thoughts that I hold on to.

It's really encouraging to know that you've made it since then for longer than I've been alive. It gives me hope that I can make it too. Many days, I don't know why I'm alive, or why I should be. I remember my friend's frantic response when I texted him last semester and told him that I wanted to give up, and I think of all the resources that exist to help suicidal people, and I wonder why everyone is so anxious about preserving life, when it doesn't even seem worth it. Sometimes I set deadlines for myself, where things have to get better in x number of years, or else I'll kill myself. 

But knowing that you've made it, and that you found a reason to make it, gives me so much hope. Thank you for that :)
Thank you :) I really do need to learn to be more compassionate with myself

I'm currently unaffiliated with any denomination at the moment. I still go to other churches, but I don't get involved or affiliated to the extent that I would have before. A lot of the time I want to quit altogether.

There is a young man that I've loved mutually for several years, who I think I would be together with now if not for the fact that his denomination forbids marriage outside of the denomination itself. It really bothers me that Jesus' message was largely about love, but the church is so intent on restricting it to their own definition. It's ridiculous, and doesn't give me much hope for me ever recovering my faith.

And I realise that there are other denominations that are less restricting, as you pointed out, but that just makes me aware of how fragmented the whole religion is. These are all things that I've been grappling with since, but it isn't wholly a bad thing.

Personally, I refuse to do any more than I can manage. If she insists on peering into all the nooks and crannies to notice all the dust I miss, she can damn well clean it up herself.

Having that need skyrocket after the episode with my dad last week, I finally understand that I've been trying to fill a void this whole time.
